name: Epilator

lead: An epilator is an electric device with rotating tweezer-like discs or springs that grab and pull several hairs out at once. It is used on legs, arms, underarms and the bikini area, with smaller heads for the face, for skin that stays smooth longer than shaving.

Because hairs are pulled out of the follicle rather than cut at the surface, new hair has to grow from beneath the skin before it appears, and results last about three to four weeks. Hair-removal reviews classify epilation as temporary. No trials of consumer epilators were identified; evidence comes from general reviews, one small comparison study and user accounts.

paras: Users epilate dry, clean skin in slow passes against the direction of growth, often after exfoliating, and repeat every few weeks. Pain is reported to be worst at first and tends to ease with repeated use.

Pain, redness, ingrown hairs and folliculitis are common. Reviews find non-permanent methods have comparable risks, and one study found no significant difference in folliculitis between manual and electric epilation.

chain: Hairs pulled out at the root
angle.text: Users epilate legs, arms, underarms and bikini area, and sometimes the face, for smooth skin that stays hairless for weeks. Hairs are pulled out at the root, so regrowth takes longer than after shaving. Pain and ingrown hairs are commonly mentioned drawbacks.

lead: An epilator is an electrical device that removes hair by mechanically grasping several hairs at once and pulling them out. The action is similar to waxing, but epilators do not use an adhesive and, unlike waxing, do not remove skin cells [1]. They are used mostly on the legs, arms, underarms and bikini area, with smaller heads for the face.

Because hairs are pulled out of the follicle rather than cut at the surface, the new hair has to grow from beneath the skin before it reappears, and results are described as lasting several weeks, longer than shaving [1][2]. Hair removal reviews classify plucking and related epilation methods as temporary, with only electrolysis labelled permanent [3]. The pulling is painful for many users, particularly on the first sessions; Wikipedia notes that regular epilation of regrowth tends to be less painful than the first treatment [1].

No clinical trials of consumer mechanical epilators were identified in the sources reviewed. Evidence comes from general reviews of hair removal, one small electrolysis-related comparison study and user accounts.
infobox: Yair Dar, Shimon Yahav and Menachem Baruch, per Grokipedia [2]

paras: Wikipedia describes four main design families. Spring-type epilators use a flexed coil spring that traps hairs as it rotates; they were the first consumer type and are still sold as manual facial devices turned by hand [1]. Rotating-disc types use metal discs that pinch hairs in a similar fashion [1]. Modern tweezer-type heads use rows of metal plates that move together and apart once per revolution so that hairs are gripped and pulled [1]. Many current models are cordless, rechargeable and designed for wet or dry use in the shower or with a cream or gel, which proponents say reduces pain and irritation [1].
Attachments commonly sold with epilators include small heads for the face and underarms, shaver heads and exfoliation heads intended to be used before and after epilation [1].

The rotating head repeatedly closes and releases around hairs, pulling them out as the device is moved across the skin. Depending on the strength and brittleness of the hair, some break at or just above the surface rather than coming out whole; these can look like sparse stubble, and the number of broken hairs is said to diminish with regular use [1].

Hair grows in cycles, and the proportion of follicles in the growth phase varies across an area. Wikipedia notes that, as with waxing, because of the phases of the growth cycle there is less regrowth after the first epilation [1].

A review of hair removal practices divides methods into depilation (removing the shaft: shaving, chemical depilatories) and epilation (removing the shaft, follicle and bulb: plucking, threading, waxing, sugaring, lasers, intense pulsed light, electrolysis and photodynamic therapy), and states that all methods are temporary except electrolysis, with each having advantages and disadvantages in efficacy and side effects [3]. Mechanical epilators fall within the plucking family of this classification.

A 1998 comparison of three electrical-energy depilation methods (radio-frequency tweezers, direct-current tweezers and needle electrolysis) in ten volunteers reported hair-count reductions of around 56 to 66 percent after nine weeks, with no significant difference between methods but lower pain scores for the tweezer devices [4]. These electrical tweezers are professional-style devices and are different from consumer rotating-head epilators, so the results are an indirect reference only.
Encyclopedic summaries state that results from epilation last up to about four weeks [2].

Pain is the most commonly reported effect. Wikipedia lists approaches that people use to reduce it, including slower speeds, relaxing the skin in a hot shower or bath, using a numbing cream, or having the area professionally waxed first [1]. Redness, ingrown hairs and folliculitis are also described for epilation [2]. A 2023 review of hair removal in the genital area discusses skin reactions and infection risks across epilation and depilation methods generally [5].
Hair removal reviews note that most studies of efficacy and adverse events are limited and based on darker hair and fairer skin [3].

The original Epilady, a spring-type device, was released in Israel in 1986 and made by Mepro at Kibbutz HaGoshrim [1]. Grokipedia credits Yair Dar, Shimon Yahav and Menachem Baruch with developing the prototype in 1985 and reports patents in 32 countries [2]. Wikipedia reports that the Remington disc-type epilator led to extensive patent litigation in Europe, including the UK case Improver Corporation v Remington Consumer Product Limited [1].

Later designs replaced the continuous spring and discs with plate-based tweezer heads, and added cordless and wet-use models [1]. Grokipedia dates a rotating-disc model called the Discrette to 1996 [2].

Epilators are discussed in grooming forums as an option between shaving and waxing: longer-lasting than razors, cheaper over time than salon waxing and usable without heating wax. A thread on the Straight Dope message board compared bikini waxing and epilator use from the perspective of people who had tried both [6]. The site's own rating records the trade-off as weeks of smooth skin at the cost of some pain.

No studies found on consumer mechanical epilators. Related research includes a 1998 comparison of three electrical depilation devices (two tweezer types and needle electrolysis) in ten volunteers [4], and a 1971 German paper on determining hair-root status with a mechanical epilator [7]. General hair-removal literature reviews are summarised above [3][5].
